chapter_title: Projecting AI Growth: Doubling Curves, Limits, and Uncertainty
learning_objective: The learner will judge whether each of six statements in an AI-written summary is supported by a source passage, correctly judging at least five of six on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** verify-the-ai-summary
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate
**Bloom Verb:** judge
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge whether each of six statements in an AI-written summary is supported by a source passage, correctly judging at least five of six on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** AI hallucination, grounding in a source, AI literacy (all defined in the section "AI Hallucination and AI Literacy" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner marks each of 6 statements as Supported or Not supported and submits it. A mark is correct when it matches the "Correct mark" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the passage is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) A confident, fluent statement is probably correct. (2) A statement that sounds plausible is supported. (3) A summary that is mostly right can be trusted whole. **Instructional Rationale:** Judging a statement requires the learner to compare it with a source, which is the central habit of AI literacy. Mixing statements that are correct, subtly changed, and invented shows that fluency gives no clue to accuracy. **Content:** Source passage shown in full (fictional, written for this chapter): "Lincoln Middle School ran a six-week pilot of a math program with 280 seventh graders. A computer randomly assigned 140 students to use the program for 30 minutes a day and 140 to continue as normal. At the end of the pilot, the program group scored an average of 34 points on a 50-point test and the comparison group scored an average of 30. The standard deviation of scores was 10 points. Six teachers were interviewed. They said the dashboard was useful, but two teachers used the tablets only on Fridays." Six statements in an AI-written summary: | # | Statement | Correct mark | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | The pilot involved 280 seventh graders. | Supported | The passage states 280 seventh graders. | | 2 | Students were assigned to groups at random. | Supported | The passage says a computer randomly assigned them. | | 3 | The program group scored 34 on average, four points above the comparison group. | Supported | The passage gives 34 and 30. | | 4 | The pilot lasted a full semester. | Not supported | The passage says six weeks, not a semester. | | 5 | All six teachers used the tablets every day. | Not supported | Two teachers used the tablets only on Fridays. | | 6 | An independent university team ran the evaluation. | Not supported | The passage does not say who ran the evaluation. | **Provenance:** The passage is the Chapter 2 pilot rewritten as a short text. The statements are illustrative. The sim must label the passage and summary "Fictional, for practice." **Rules:** Each statement has exactly one correct mark. A statement is scored on its first submitted mark only. The score counts first-attempt correct marks out of 6. Mastery is a score >= 5. Missing information counts as Not supported. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads the passage and the six statements. 2. For each statement, the learner marks Supported or Not supported and submits. The sim marks it and shows the feedback and the matching sentence of the passage, if any. 3. If incorrect, the learner may re-mark; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct mark and reason are shown. 4. After all 6, the sim shows the score. 5. The learner should notice that statement 6 sounds reasonable but has no support in the passage. **Feedback:** 6 statements, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [mark]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Look for a sentence in the passage that says this. [Why text]." After the second attempt the correct mark is revealed and the statement counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 6" is shown. Final message for a score >= 5: "You checked the summary against its source." For a score < 5: "Reread the passage and try again." **Starting State:** The passage and the first statement are shown, with the score "First-try correct: 0 of 6," and the prompt "Does the passage support this statement?" **Chapter Anchors:** The passage uses the Chapter 2 pilot figures: 280 students, 140 per group, 30 minutes a day, six weeks, averages of 34 and 30, standard deviation 10, and six teachers. The mastery bar is 5 of 6.
